payload.name: Past visits only when enumerating visited places
payload.description: Use when a question asks which places a person has been to, visited, or traveled to; require past completed presence and exclude plans or aspirational mentions.
content: When a question asks for locations a person 'has been to' or 'visited', list only memories that document a completed past physical presence (event with past timestamp or past-tense activity). Exclude plan memories, future-dated intentions, and aspirational statements even if the person is excited or has added them to a travel list.

Do not infer presence from reading about a place, joining a travel-related group, or discussing a place; require an explicit activity at the location (e.g., visited, toured, took a photo in, hiked in).
Before finalizing, run at least one additional search combining the person's name with activity terms that imply presence (photo, trip, visited, went, hiked), not only the verbatim query.

candidates.solves: Agents answering 'which places has X been to?' often mix future plans and aspirational reading into the list and miss implicit evidence such as photos. This skill adds a reusable rule: for past-travel questions, a location counts only with a completed event of physical presence, and searches should include activity terms that imply presence. It applies to any future enumeration of visited locations; it does not apply to questions about planned or desired destinations.

payload.name: Include event memories for hobby-duration questions
payload.description: When a question asks how long someone has been doing a hobby/practice/activity, include event memory kind in searches; do not restrict to preference/state only.
content: For duration questions about an ongoing activity (how long, for how many years, since when), run at least one search with memory_kinds including 'event' (with preference/state), because duration facts are often stored as event records.
If the initial preference/state-only search returns no duration, retry with event kind before answering 'no information'.

candidates.solves: Duration questions about a person's hobby or activity were missed because searches restricted memory_kinds to preference/state, while the duration fact was stored as an event record (e.g., 'has been practicing yoga for three years'). The reusable pattern: any 'how long has X been doing Y' query must include event memories, since duration facts for ongoing activities often live in events, not only in preference/state records.

payload.name: Search concrete follow-up action after described event
payload.description: When a question asks what activity someone did after a described event and the first search returns only the event/planning memory, run additional searches with concrete follow-up action terms before answering.
content: When a question asks what X did after an event (e.g., after reading about Y), do not treat a memory that only describes X's reading, planning, or interest around that event as evidence of the post-event activity itself.

Run additional hybrid or keyword searches combining the subject and the event's date window with concrete consequential-action vocabulary such as 'visited', 'went to', 'contacted', 'booked', 'researched', 'applied', 'agency', 'office', 'class', or 'requirements'.

If retrieved post-event memories share the event date but not its topic words, inspect them for explicit actions; continue searching until a memory states the concrete follow-up activity rather than answering from the event-description memory.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what activity someone did after a described event, the agent may over-anchor on the event's topic words and answer from a memory that describes the event or planning rather than the actual follow-up action, which is stored with different vocabulary. This skill applies to any future post-event activity question where the first retrieval returns the event/planning memory but not the concrete consequential action.

payload.name: Broaden memory kinds for recently completed activities
payload.description: When a query asks what someone recently finished, completed, read, watched, or did (e.g., just finished reading), do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' and 'state' because such facts are often stored as preferences.
content: If a question asks about a person's recently completed activity (e.g., just finished reading, recently finished, completed), set memory_kinds to include 'event', 'preference', and 'state', or omit the memory_kinds filter, since such facts are frequently stored as preference or state memories rather than events.
If an initial search restricted to 'event' returns no supporting evidence for that question, retry with broader memory_kinds (especially 'preference') before answering 'no information available'.

candidates.solves: The agent missed the answer because it restricted memory_kinds to 'event', while the supporting memory was a 'preference'. Reusable rule: for queries about recently completed activities (e.g., just finished reading, recently finished), broaden memory_kinds to include 'preference' and 'state' in addition to 'event'; applies to any future question asking what someone recently finished, read, watched, or completed.

payload.name: Event-activity terms for time-window location queries
payload.description: When a question asks where someone was or what they did in a past time window, search with travel/activity event terms and relative-time references, not only location words.
content: When a question asks where a person was or what they did in a past time window (e.g., 'the week before <date>'), do not limit searches to location words (where, whereabouts, location); also search with event/activity vocabulary such as trip, visited, traveled, went to, attended, and place names.

Include relative-time expressions (last week, last Friday, yesterday) in retrieval and resolve them to concrete dates from the session/message timestamp; treat a memory whose world_start falls within the requested window as eligible evidence even if its text expresses time relatively.
Before answering 'no information' for such a window/location question, run at least one additional search combining the subject with activity and relative-time terms.

candidates.solves: Retrieval fails when a past-window location question is searched only with location wording, missing event memories that phrase time relatively and place via activity. Adding travel/activity vocabulary and resolving relative-time references to dates transfers to any future question asking where someone was or what they did in a past period, for any person, place, or date.

payload.name: Activity-term expansion for travel-destination retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks where someone traveled/went during a time period, use activity-term query expansion and subject-only searches to retrieve location memories that do not contain the words 'travel' or the companion's role.
content: When a question asks where a person went/traveled for a period, do not limit keywords to 'travel'/'trip' or to the companion's role; the supporting memory may describe the event with activity terms such as 'retreat', 'vacation', 'getaway', 'visit', or 'attended'.

Run additional retrieval using the subject's name and the time window (e.g., name + month/year) plus activity-related terms, and also a variant without the companion's role so that a memory describing the subject alone can surface.
Before answering, verify that the candidate memory's time window overlaps the question's time period; a memory outside that window is not evidence, even if it mentions a similar location or activity.

candidates.solves: When a question asks where someone traveled or went for a time period, retrieval over-anchors on surface terms like 'travel' or the companion's role and misses memories that describe the event as an activity (e.g., retreat, vacation) in a location without those words. This skill directs query expansion with activity vocabulary and subject-only searches, and requires time-window overlap verification, so future travel-destination questions can surface the correct evidence.

payload.name: Retrieve intention-expressing memories for open-ended plan questions
payload.description: When a question asks what projects or plans a person has without naming a specific domain, use intention verbs (plans to, aims to, wants to, interested in, hopes to) in query expansions and treat memories expressing goals or interests as evidence of plans.
content: When a question asks open-endedly about someone's projects or plans (e.g., 'what is X planning?', 'what projects does X have?') without naming the domain, do not limit the search to the literal words 'project' or 'plan'. Expand the query with intention verbs and aspiration phrases such as 'plans to', 'aims to', 'wants to', 'interested in', 'hopes to', 'intends to', 'focusing on', 'developing', 'finding ways to'.

Include event memories even if their predicate is not 'project' (e.g., 'conversation', 'goal', 'interest') when the content describes future intentions or aspirations, and do not require the memory text to contain the word 'project' or 'plan'.

Before answering a 'what projects/plans' question, verify that the supporting memories express future intention or aspiration (e.g., 'plans to', 'wants to', 'aims to') rather than merely describing an ongoing/past project. If the only retrieved memories are generic 'a project' without a topic, run an additional search with the intention-verb expansions.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that retrieval for an open-ended 'what projects' question relied on literal 'project/plan' terms and stopped after one search, missing memories that convey the person's intentions through aspiration verbs (e.g., 'interested in', 'aims to', 'wants to') and conversation events. The abstraction is a reusable rule to expand with intention language and to accept such memories as evidence of plans, which transfers to any future question asking broadly about someone's planned work, goals, or initiatives.

payload.name: Resume-evidence pair for activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks what activity someone resumed, took up again, or returned to after a long time, search for past hobby/interest evidence and pair it with a recent activity event before answering.
content: If a question asks what activity someone resumed, took up again, or returned to after a long time/gap, search for preference and profile memories about past hobbies/interests (e.g., '<person> used to love <activity>', '<person> hobby') as well as event memories, before answering.

Use a resumption answer only when evidence includes both a past absence/gap statement for the activity and a later event/state of the same activity; a single same-period event is not sufficient to show a resumed activity.
If the first retrieval surfaces only unrelated same-period events, re-search with candidate activity terms and re-check preference/state memories before selecting an answer.

candidates.solves: An agent can mistake an unrelated event in the target period for the resumed activity. For questions using resume, take up again, return to, after a long time, or after a gap, require both a past absence/gap statement and a later event/state of the same activity. Does not apply to ordinary dated-activity questions without a resumption cue.

payload.name: distinguish-done-vs-interested-activities
payload.description: When a question asks what activities a person has done (completed, participated in, attended) rather than what they are interested in or plan to try, use this skill to guide retrieval and evidence judgment.
content: If the question asks what activities someone has done (e.g., 'has [subject] done', 'activities [subject] has participated in'), run multiple searches with concrete activity terms across event, preference, and plan memories before answering; do not stop after one search.

Treat only memories with explicit participation verbs ('went', 'attended', 'participated in', 'did', 'took part in') as evidence of completed activities; do not count expressions of interest, desire, or future plans ('interested in trying', 'wants to try', 'plans to') as activities done.

For each candidate activity surfaced, run a follow-up keyword search for that activity name to verify actual participation; if a memory mixes an activity the person did with one they want to try, include only the participated item.

candidates.solves: A question asked which activities a person had done, but the retrieval stopped after finding one activity and the answer included activities the person only expressed interest in trying, while missing a separate memory of an actual activity. The reusable mechanism is treating interest or intention as evidence of completion and not exhaustively searching for concrete activity names. This applies to any future question asking what activities, hobbies, or experiences someone has actually participated in or completed versus merely considered or planned.

payload.name: Include plan memories for location-period queries
payload.description: When a question asks where someone was during a date range, search plan memories and avoid strict time-window filters that exclude travel/location records.
content: When a question asks about a person's location or whereabouts during a date range, do not restrict memory_kinds to event and state; include plan memories, because past travel or visits may be recorded in plan or enriched plan memories.

Avoid using a strict time window as a hard filter for location queries; first search without time restrictions or with a broad time range, then evaluate temporal relevance from memory text and timestamps, since a plan memory's world_start may be after the queried period while its text describes an earlier trip.

Before answering a location question, require a memory that explicitly names the place; do not infer location from related events such as a team reunion or game that do not state a city, and keep searching with place-oriented terms like 'traveled to', 'visited', 'was in', or 'stayed' if explicit location evidence is missing.

candidates.solves: When a question asks where someone was during a date range, retrieval may miss the answer because location/travel information is stored in a plan or enriched plan memory whose world_start lies outside the queried window, and because search filters restricted memory kinds to event/state. This rule generalizes to any future location/whereabouts question: broaden kind and time filters so plan memories containing explicit places are considered, and avoid answering from an event that does not name a location.

payload.name: Search travel events for city-enumeration questions
payload.description: When a question asks which cities/places a person visited or mentioned visiting, even to another person, search travel/event memories and do not require the audience name or the word 'visit'.
content: If a question enumerates cities/places a person visited or mentioned visiting (e.g., 'Which US cities does X mention visiting to Y?'), run at least one hybrid search combining the person's name with travel/event terms such as 'traveled to', 'visited', 'event in', 'trip to', and 'favorite city'; do not require the audience's name or the word 'mention' to appear.

Treat event memories that locate the person in a city (upcoming games, trips, visits, 'favorite city to explore') as evidence for city visitation even when the memory does not name the audience or use the word 'visit'.
Before answering with a city list, run a supplementary search for each already-found city paired with the person's name to catch additional city memories the first query missed.

candidates.solves: Search over-anchored on the audience and the surface verb 'visiting', so a city memory stored as an event (e.g., an upcoming game in a favorite city) was never retrieved. The reusable fix is to retrieve the person's travel/event memories independently of the audience when a question enumerates cities/places visited or mentioned visiting. This applies to future 'which cities did X visit/mention to Y' questions where location evidence may live in event memories without the audience's name.

payload.name: SearchProfileKindsForMembershipQueries
payload.description: When a question asks what classes, courses, groups, workshops, or organizations a person has joined, attended, or participates in, include profile and state memory kinds, not only event/plan.
content: When answering what classes, courses, groups, workshops, or memberships a person has joined/attends/participates in, do not restrict memory_kinds to event and plan; also search profile, state, and preference kinds because ongoing affiliations are often stored there.

Run at least one complementary search using membership phrasing such as 'is a member of', 'joined', 'participates in', or 'signed up for' without a restrictive memory-kind filter, then aggregate all named classes/groups from every retrieved memory before answering.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure: the agent answered a question about joined classes/groups using only event/plan memory kinds and missed a profile memory recording an ongoing group membership. Sustained memberships, affiliations, and enrolled courses are frequently stored as profile/state facts rather than one-off events, so memory-kind restrictions hide them. This rule applies to any future question asking what classes, courses, groups, workshops, or organizations a person has joined, attended, or participates in.

payload.name: Search descriptive adjectives for habitual activity places
payload.description: When a question asks what type of place a person regularly meditates, relaxes, or practices wellness activities, and first results show only named retreats or generic memories.
content: Run an additional search combining the person's name, the activity, and descriptive location adjectives like tranquil, quiet, peaceful, nearby, or favorite.
Prefer a current habitual setting memory over a past named destination when the question implies recurring practice; use memory kind and world_start/world_end to distinguish.
Do not choose the most explicit place name; require a memory connecting the person, the activity, and a place descriptor.

candidates.solves: A literal activity+place search missed a memory describing the habitual spot as 'nearby tranquil spot' and selected a one-time retreat instead. This happens when a question asks for a regular activity's location and the correct memory uses descriptive adjectives rather than a place noun. The rule applies to wellness/leisure activities with one-time destination distractors.

payload.name: Enumerate places visited in a specific time window
payload.description: When a question asks which places (or all places) a person visited during a specific month or period, gather every candidate location memory, verify timestamps, and expand searches with discovered place and activity terms before answering.
content: When a question asks which places a person visited in a specific time window, treat it as an enumeration task: keep searching until follow-up queries stop surfacing new candidate place memories, and do not answer from the first retrieved location alone.

For each retrieved travel/activity memory, extract its named places and activity descriptors (e.g., road trip, skiing, hiking) and use those as additional query terms in later searches instead of reusing the original query or the first place name.

Before counting a candidate place, verify its memory world_start/world_end falls within the requested period; exclude any candidate whose timestamp is outside the window even if it is the only or highest-scoring result.
When multiple candidates have in-period evidence, include all distinct places in the answer rather than selecting a single one.

candidates.solves: Future questions that ask which places (including 'which places...', 'all places...') a person visited during a specific month or period. The diagnosed cause is that the agent anchored on the first retrieved location, used an out-of-window memory as evidence, and missed other in-window places because follow-up searches reused the original query rather than terms mined from retrieved memories. The rule transfers to any location enumeration question with a temporal constraint; it does not apply to open-ended location questions without a time window.

payload.name: Search concrete project names for category questions
payload.description: When a question asks what kind(s) or type(s) of projects, items, or work someone has done, search using concrete object/domain terms and enumerate distinct named projects before answering.
content: When a question asks what kind(s) or type(s) of projects, items, or work a person has done, treat one generic query as insufficient; it can return vague 'project' memories instead of concrete named projects.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search using concrete object nouns or domain-specific project terms (not only the generic category label), with memory_kinds ['event','plan'] before answering.
Enumerate distinct named projects from all retrieved event/plan memories; include a specific named project even if its memory was not the top-ranked hit.

candidates.solves: A category question such as 'what kind of engineering projects has this person worked on?' often receives one generic search, so vague 'project' memories crowd out concrete named projects. The failure is a retrieval rule gap: category-enumeration questions need object-level searches and enumeration of distinct named memories. The rule applies to any question asking kinds/types of projects, creative work, or owned items, but not to questions about a single project or a numeric count.

payload.name: Physical-transformation query vocabulary expansion
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's physical transformation or appearance change in a date range, and initial retrieval returns no direct evidence, use concrete appearance-change terms and re-search before answering.
content: When a question asks what physical transformation or appearance change someone underwent in a time period, do not rely only on abstract phrases like 'physical transformation' or 'appearance change'; run additional searches using concrete change verbs and nouns (dyed, colored, hair, tattoo, piercing, shaved, cut, styled, gained/lost weight, glasses).

Treat an appearance-change memory as one whose text may not contain the abstract category label or exact date-range wording; after an initial search returns only unrelated events, issue another search combining the subject, concrete appearance-change vocabulary, and the target time window (or world_start filter) before concluding no information.

Do not answer 'No information available' after a single top-k retrieval for a physical-change question; require at least one expanded concrete-term search and inspect event memories with world_start inside the target period as potential evidence.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that a query built only from the abstract category term missed the concrete stored event, and the agent stopped after one unfruitful search. The reusable mechanism is abstract-question vocabulary mismatch for appearance-change events, which applies whenever a future question asks what physical/appearance change a person underwent in a dated window. The rule forces concrete-term expansion and at least one additional search before answering no-information.

payload.name: EnumerateAdditionalItemsViaCategorySearches
payload.description: When answering enumeration questions about read/watched/played/consumed items, after an initial search returns some items, run additional searches for generic category descriptions before finalizing.
content: If the question asks for a list or enumeration of items a person has read, watched, played, or consumed, do not finalize the answer after one search even if it returns some concrete items.

Run additional hybrid or keyword searches pairing the activity with generic category descriptors likely present in memories (e.g., 'non-fiction', 'series', 'fantasy', 'personal development', 'mystery') and inspect both event and preference memories for items described by category.
Aggregate all distinct named or clearly described items from all searches before composing the answer; if only one search was performed, treat the list as potentially incomplete.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for an enumeration of items a person has read/watched/played/consumed, an initial search may return some named items yet miss memories that describe additional items by category. The diagnosed failure was stopping after one retrieval and omitting category-described books. Applies to any future list/enumeration query where relevant memories may describe items generically; run supplementary searches before answering.

payload.name: Ensure per-person item evidence for activity-enhancement questions
payload.description: When a question asks what ways, methods, or items multiple people use to enhance or improve an activity, verify each named person has concrete item evidence and run targeted per-person preference/event searches if one has only generic activity memories.
content: When the question asks what ways or items people use to enhance/improve an activity, treat it as requiring concrete enhancers for each named person, not merely the activity itself.

After retrieval, map evidence to each named person. If a person has only generic activity memories, run a supplementary hybrid search with that person's name, the activity, and common enhancement-item terms (e.g., scents, music, equipment, atmosphere, 'prefers', 'purchased'), including preference and event memory kinds.
Do not answer until every named person either has a concrete enhancement item in evidence or a targeted per-person search has been attempted.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because a multi-person 'how do they enhance X' question was answered from generic activity memories, missing one person's concrete enhancement items stored in preference/event memories. The reusable rule is to verify per-person evidence of concrete enhancers and run targeted per-person item searches before answering. It applies to future questions asking what ways/methods/items multiple people use to enhance or improve an activity; it does not apply to questions seeking only general activities without specific enhancement items.

payload.name: EnumerateAllItemsForListQuestions
payload.description: When a user asks for a list of items (e.g., classes, courses, activities, hobbies) that a person took, attended, or is involved in, do not answer after finding one relevant memory; search multiple phrasings and memory kinds and aggregate all distinct items.
content: When a question asks for a list of items (e.g., 'what are the classes/courses/activities/hobbies'), treat it as an enumeration request: do not stop after the first supporting memory or after a single search.

Run multiple searches with varied phrasings and synonyms (e.g., class, course, workshop, training, seminar, activity) and include relevant memory kinds such as 'event', 'profile', and 'state'; for enrollments or sign-ups, include 'event' memories with future world_start if the query also covers planned or registered items.

Before answering, gather all distinct items from the combined retrieved set; if the retrieved set lacks enough distinct items or the question implies multiple, issue additional searches before finalizing.

candidates.solves: When a question asks to enumerate a person's items (e.g., classes taken, courses attended, activities, hobbies), the diagnosed failure was answering from the first retrieved memory only, missing other supported items. The reusable mechanism is that plural-list questions require multiple synonym searches and cross-kind evidence aggregation before answering. This applies to any future list-eliciting query about a person's activities, courses, or possessions, but not to questions seeking a single fact or a yes/no confirmation.

payload.name: Search collection-specific vocabulary for collection enumeration
payload.description: Use when a question asks what items a person collects or what their collection includes; run supplementary searches using collection terms and concrete category items.
content: If a question asks what items a person collects or what their collection includes, do not answer from one generic search like 'items <person> collects'. Run additional hybrid searches with collection-specific phrasings: '<person> collection', '<person> collects', '<person> likes to collect', and '<person> enjoys collecting'.

Before finalizing, generate concrete collectible category terms from the person's interests and run at least one search combining those terms with the person's name; preference memories may mention an item only as an enjoyment/interest (e.g., 'enjoys X', 'interested in X') without using the word 'collect'.
When gathering candidates, include distinct items named in preference memories as collection evidence even if the memory does not explicitly say the person collects them.

candidates.solves: Questions enumerating a person's collected items often fail with one generic 'items <person> collects' query because preference memories describe collections indirectly (e.g., 'collection of sneakers', 'enjoys fantasy movies'). This skill adds collection-specific query variants and category-term searches so future questions retrieve all indirectly stated collectibles. Applies to 'what does X collect' questions, not to non-collection enumerations like counts of owned items.

payload.name: SearchActivityFactsAcrossPredicates
payload.description: When answering what activities/hobbies a person pursues (with or without an excluded topic), supplement structured predicate='activity' searches with semantic/free-text searches for concrete activity terms across memory kinds.
content: When a question asks what activities or hobbies a person pursues (including 'besides', 'apart from', or 'other than' an excluded topic), do not rely only on structured queries with predicate='activity'; activity facts are often embedded in event/preference/state memories with other predicates or in free-text descriptions.

Run at least one hybrid or semantic/free-text search combining the person's name with concrete activity vocabulary (e.g., running, biking, art, gardening, surfing) and without requiring the words 'activity' or 'hobby' to appear.

Before answering, if the retrieved set is missing concrete activities, widen memory_kinds beyond 'event' to include 'preference', 'profile', and 'state', and re-search each concrete activity name that appears anywhere in the session or evidence.

candidates.solves: When generic 'activities' searches miss concrete activities because facts are stored under non-activity predicates (e.g., 'discovered surfing', 'ran a gardening class'), the answer becomes incomplete. This rule supplements structured predicate='activity' queries with semantic/free-text searches for concrete activity terms and checks all memory kinds. Applies to future activity/hobby questions, including 'besides X' variants.

payload.name: SearchValueTermsForAttributeQuestions
payload.description: When a question asks for a concrete attribute value of a person's possessions or works (e.g., dog breeds, car make, music genre) and a search using only the category noun returns generic memories, run additional searches using likely value terms before answering.
content: When a question asks for the value of an attribute (breed, type, make, model, genre, cuisine), do not stop after a single search that repeats only the attribute noun; the supporting memory may express the value directly, e.g., 'Lab mix' or 'Chihuahua mix', without the noun.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search using concrete value terms and synonyms (for dog breeds: 'Lab', 'Chihuahua', 'mix', 'mongrel'; for other attributes: likely brand/type/style words), and inspect low-scoring results that contain these values.

Before answering from a generic memory or saying no information, check for a more specific memory about the same subject (e.g., one listing individual pets and their breeds), and inspect its versions if the current version lacks detail.

candidates.solves: The first search for 'breeds of Audrey's dogs' returned only generic dog-care memories because the supporting memory stated 'Lab mixes' and 'Chihuahua mixes' without the word 'breeds'. The reusable mechanism is that attribute questions are answered by concrete value terms, not only the category noun; this rule applies to any future question asking about breeds, types, makes, models, genres, or cuisines where evidence may use examples instead of the umbrella term.

payload.name: EnumerateConcreteActivityTypesForCategoryQueries
payload.description: When a question asks what kinds/types of activities a person participates in within a domain (e.g., professional, academic, volunteer, creative), enumerate and search for concrete activity types like conference, workshop, internship, course, or presentation before answering.
content: When the question asks about types/kinds of activities in a domain, do not search only with the abstract category phrase. Generate a list of concrete activity types common to that domain and run at least one search per type using participation phrasing (e.g., '[subject] presented at', '[subject] attends', '[subject] interned at').

Before finalizing, verify the answer covers every enumerated activity type that has supporting evidence. If initial results lack some types, search for them explicitly, because memories often store the concrete activity (e.g., 'presented at a virtual conference') without the category label.

candidates.solves: Open-ended questions asking what kinds of activities someone participates in are answered after searching only the abstract category phrase, so memories naming concrete instances (e.g., 'presented at a virtual conference') are missed. This skill forces explicit enumeration and search for common concrete activity types in the domain before sufficiency is judged. Applies to any activity-type domain; not needed when the user already names a specific activity.

payload.name: Count items despite shared person names
payload.description: Use when counting how many of an item a person owns and a retrieved memory contains a name that also appears as a person.
content: When counting owned items and a name in the retrieved memory also refers to a person, do not exclude that name from the item count solely because of the other role.
Use context to identify item-role occurrences: phrases like 'adopted [name]', 'owns [name]', 'take [name1] and [name2] to the park', or a list of the person's pets/items.
If the name is used in an item context in any memory, count it as a separate owned item even if another memory uses the same name for a person.

candidates.solves: The agent undercounted owned items because a name that also referred to a person was excluded from the item count, even though the same memory listed that name among the owned pets. This rule abstracts the ambiguous shared-name mechanism and applies to any owned-item count where a person and an item share a name, preventing similar undercounting.

payload.name: Include event memories for commonality queries
payload.description: When a question asks what two or more entities share or have in common, include event and plan memories in retrieval; do not restrict memory_kinds to profile or preference.
content: For intersection queries asking what two or more entities have in common, set memory_kinds to include 'event' (and 'plan' or 'state' when relevant) in addition to 'profile' and 'preference'; shared circumstances such as job changes, business launches, or life milestones are typically stored as event or plan memories.

If an initial commonality search returns only one entity's preferences or profiles, run separate per-entity searches without the restrictive memory_kinds filter and examine event memories before concluding no commonality.

candidates.solves: The agent answered a two-person commonality question using only profile/preference memories, missing shared life events such as job loss and starting a business. The reusable failure is narrowing memory_kinds for intersection queries; commonalities are often episodic. Future multi-entity 'have in common' questions should broaden retrieval to event and plan memories, regardless of the people or topics involved.

payload.name: Pre-milestone problems from active-search memories
payload.description: When a question asks about problems or difficulties someone faced before a milestone (adoption, move, purchase, start), search for their active search/requirements/constraints rather than only literal problem words.
content: When a question asks what problems, difficulties, or challenges a person faced before a milestone event, run an additional search using concrete active-search and requirement phrases such as 'looking for', 'searching for', 'seeking', 'needed', 'wanted', 'finding', plus likely domain criteria, instead of only searching 'problems/issues/challenges'.

Treat memories that describe the person's active search or explicit constraints before the event (e.g., suitability for their living situation, location near desired amenities) as evidence of pre-milestone problems, even if the word problem does not appear.

candidates.solves: The failure was answering 'no information' after querying only literal problem words, while the supporting memory described the person's active search requirements before a milestone. Pre-milestone obstacles are often stored as active-search or constraint statements, not as negative labels. Future questions about problems/difficulties before an event should also retrieve concrete search/requirement vocabulary and treat it as evidence.

payload.name: Expand artifact keywords for method-of-activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks how a person remembers, records, organizes, or otherwise manages something, and initial retrieval returns only generic memories, rerun with concrete artifact nouns (board, notebook, photo, album) and inspect returned event memories.
content: If a question asks what a person does to remember, record, track, or organize something, do not answer from a single search; run additional hybrid/keyword searches pairing the person's name with concrete artifact nouns that could embody the method (e.g., notebook, journal, photo, board, album, calendar).
Inspect event memories returned by these artifact-focused searches even when they do not explicitly mention the queried activity, because the artifact often indicates the method.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because retrieval only used 'remember'/'happy memories' and missed an event memory about a cork board that concretely represents the method. Existing skills broaden memory_kinds but do not instruct query expansion with artifact nouns. The rule applies to future 'how does X do Y' questions (remembering, recording, organizing) where evidence may be stored as event memories about physical objects; it does not apply when the method is already explicit in initial retrieval.

payload.name: Concrete re-search for abstract activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks when or how someone did something described with abstract/functional wording (e.g., 'fun indoor area') and the first search returns no close match, use concrete object and action synonyms in additional searches before concluding the answer is unavailable.
content: If a question asks about an activity using abstract or evaluative wording (e.g., 'made a fun indoor area', 'rewarding experience') and the first retrieval does not surface a memory with a clear match, do not answer 'no information' yet. Run additional hybrid/keyword searches built from concrete nouns and verbs the stored memory is likely to use (e.g., for indoor area: bed, toys, pads, crate, playpen; for making: set up, prepare, create, build).
Include structured searches on the subject entity and relevant predicates (event, preparation, plan) to catch memories whose wording differs from the question but which describe the same activity.

When the question asks for a time, use the world_start of the most concrete matching memory as the answer basis if no other memory is more precise; do not require the memory to use the question's exact wording.

candidates.solves: The search failed because the question's functional wording ('fun indoor area') did not lexically overlap with the stored memory's concrete wording ('safe space with bed, toys, puppy pads'), and the agent stopped after one search. This skill teaches the agent to bridge abstract-to-concrete vocabulary with additional synonym and structured searches before concluding evidence is missing. It applies to any access question that describes an event/activity with evaluative or functional language instead of the concrete terms in memory.

payload.name: Attribute-specific retrieval for role and position questions
payload.description: When a question asks for a specific attribute such as position, role, team, or title in connection with an action like signing or joining, use this to avoid answering from unrelated activity memories.
content: If a question asks for a specific attribute (e.g., position, role, team, title) tied to an action (e.g., signed with, joined, hired, appointed), run a targeted search that includes the subject, the action verb, and the attribute term (e.g., 'John signed position'), not just a paraphrase of the whole question.

If initial results contain memories about related activities (e.g., playing, mentoring) but none explicitly state the requested attribute, do not answer from those; search plan and event memories with the attribute term and concrete value candidates (e.g., known team names, position names) before finalizing.
Before answering an attribute question, verify that the selected evidence memory explicitly states the requested attribute; if it does not, treat the evidence as insufficient and continue searching.

candidates.solves: When asking for a specific attribute (position, role, team) tied to an action like signing or joining, retrieval can return related activity memories that lack that attribute, and the agent may answer from unrelated evidence. This skill applies to role, position, or affiliation questions where the correct fact is stored; it does not cover general activity or current-status questions.

payload.name: Search event memories for monetized passions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone loves and can make money from (earn, monetize, income, prize), also search event memories with concrete earning/competition terms before answering.
content: When a question asks what a person loves or enjoys and can make money from (e.g., monetize, earn, income, prize), do not restrict memory kinds to preference/state; run an additional search over memory_kind=event using concrete terms such as 'tournament', 'competition', 'won', 'prize', 'earned', 'paid', 'income' for that person.

If an event memory describes a win or a paid activity connected to a passion, treat it as direct evidence even when the question is phrased in terms of likes or loves; inspect the newest version of each returned memory before answering.
Do not answer from preference restatements of behavior alone when event memories about earnings may exist; run the event-kind search before concluding evidence is insufficient.

candidates.solves: Questions pairing enjoyment with monetization were answered only from preference/state memories although the decisive evidence was an enriched event memory of winning and earning. The mechanism is restricting retrieval to subjective kinds and omitting income/competition terms. Future questions joining love and money should include event-kind searches with won, prize, earned, paid, tournament; not enjoyment-only questions.

payload.name: Breakage-Enumeration Synonym Expansion
payload.description: When a question asks what things/items someone had broken or damaged and initial retrieval returns no direct 'broken' memory, use this to expand search terms before answering.
content: When a question asks what kinds of things a person had broken or damaged (e.g., 'what broke down', 'what was damaged', 'what things did X have broken'), do not conclude 'no information' after one literal search; supporting memories may use 'broke down', 'breakdown', 'accident', 'malfunction', 'issue', 'damaged', or 'repair'.

Run additional keyword or structured searches combining the person's name with breakage synonyms (broke, broken, broke down, breakdown, accident, malfunction, damage, issue, repair) and likely object categories (car, vehicle, bike, phone, appliance, device).
Check sufficiency after each search; continue until no new distinct broken/damaged items appear, and cite only memories that explicitly state an item was broken, damaged, or broke down.

candidates.solves: The Access agent answered 'no information' after a single literal search for 'broken' even though a memory stated Evan's new Prius 'broke down'. The reusable failure is premature no-info on enumerative damage questions when memory wording differs from query wording. This skill applies to future questions asking what things/items a person had broken, damaged, or had fail, requiring synonym expansion and sufficiency checks before concluding no evidence.

payload.name: Search intolerance and dietary restrictions for allergy questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone is allergic to or cannot eat/drink due to allergies or intolerances, use broader retrieval: include preference/event memories and query terms like intolerant, cannot have, dairy-free, avoids, not only the word allergy.
content: During retrieval for allergy or dietary-restriction questions, include both 'preference' and 'event' memory kinds (or omit the memory_kind filter), and expand queries with intolerance/avoidance terms such as 'intolerant', 'cannot have', 'dairy-free', 'avoids'.

Treat memories that explicitly state intolerance or inability to consume a substance as direct evidence for an allergy or restriction answer, even if the word 'allergy' is absent and the memory is stored as a preference.

candidates.solves: Allergy queries that rely only on the literal word 'allergy' miss preference memories stating an intolerance or dietary avoidance (e.g., lactose intolerant, cannot have dairy). This Skill fixes that by requiring broader memory_kind coverage and intolerance/avoidance query expansions before answering. It applies to allergy or health-restriction questions, not ordinary taste/preference questions.

payload.name: Search event-achievement details for category-item lists
payload.description: When a question asks for specific items in a category a person engages with, and initial generic searches return only broad statements, run targeted searches pairing the person with the category and engagement/achievement terms (won, played), and inspect event/achievement memories before answering.
content: If a question asks for specific items in a category (e.g., video games, movies, books) a person engages with, do not answer from broad hobby or preference statements alone.

Run targeted searches pairing the subject with the category and engagement/achievement terms (e.g., '<person> played/won <category>', '<person> <category> tournament'), and inspect event and achievement memories for named items.
Only answer 'No information available' after such targeted event/achievement searches also fail to surface any named category items.

candidates.solves: Category-item list questions often retrieve only broad hobby/event statements while the named items are stored in event/achievement memories (e.g., winning a tournament 'playing Street Fighter'). The rule requires running targeted searches pairing the subject with the category and concrete engagement/achievement terms, and inspecting event/achievement memories before answering 'No information available'. Applies to any question asking for specific instances of a category a person engages with, not to questions answerable from broad preferences alone.

payload.name: Multi-angle retrieval for inspiration-source questions
payload.description: When a question asks what a person is inspired by, influenced by, or draws creative ideas from, use follow-up searches beyond literal 'inspired by' before answering.
content: When a question asks what someone is inspired by or where they get ideas, do not stop after a single hybrid search for 'inspired by' or 'inspiration'; relevant memories often do not contain those words.

Run at least one follow-up search using source descriptors and predicates such as validation/recognition, personal history or childhood stories, people they know, things they observe, imagination, creative process, and achievement events; include memory kinds profile, event, plan, and preference.
Before answering, judge sufficiency against all candidate source memories and do not finalize until either a broad set is collected or exhaustive multi-angle searches have been attempted.

candidates.solves: Questions asking what a person is inspired by often miss memories stored under varied source predicates rather than the literal word 'inspire'. Cause: stopping after one literal hybrid search. This Skill mandates multi-angle follow-up searches across source descriptors and memory kinds before answering. Applies to future inspiration/influence-source questions for any person, not to single-fact queries or answers already explicit in evidence.

payload.name: Count Created Works via Completion Events
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many creative works a person has written, created, completed, or produced.
content: When asked how many creative works a person has written/created/completed, search with creation and completion vocabulary: wrote/written/writing, created, completed, finished, just finished, plus artifact synonyms (screenplay/script/book/song/film/project) and ordinals (first, second, another).

Treat as distinct works any memories that name a separate artifact, including completion milestones and current writing plans; merge memories that refer to the same work from different angles before counting.
If the first search returns only submission, showing, or rejection events, run an additional search for completion milestone terms before finalizing the count.

candidates.solves: Failure caused by counting only submission/showing events and missing a distinct completion memory because queries used ownership vocabulary. Abstract rule: for 'how many X has Y written/created/completed', search creation/completion terms and artifact synonyms, include plan/completion memories naming distinct works, and merge same-work references before counting. Applies to counts of written/created works generally; not to ownership counts.

payload.name: Include plan memories when retrieving creative work inspiration
payload.description: When a question asks what inspired, motivated, or a creative work is about and includes a person or date, include plan and preference/profile memory kinds in retrieval; ongoing works are often stored as plans, not events.
content: When the user asks about the inspiration, motivation, or subject of a specific creative work (screenplay, book, film, project), do not restrict memory_kinds to event; include plan, preference, and profile, because ongoing or newly started works are often stored as plan memories.

If the question includes a date, run at least one search treating that date as the world_start/filter for plan memories, and combine it with the subject and creative-work terms; do not rely only on event-kind searches.

Before answering, require a retrieved memory that explicitly states the inspiration or subject; circumstantial memories such as favorite films or general writing enjoyment are not sufficient evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what inspired or motivated a specific creative work (screenplay, book, film, project) at a date, the supporting memory is often a plan memory of an ongoing work, not an event. Restricting memory_kinds to event misses it, as happened when the agent searched only events and answered from a favorite film. Future inspiration/subject questions about current creative works should include plan memories and date-aligned retrieval; this does not apply to completed-work achievement retrieval already covered by creative-work skills.

payload.name: SearchAllWritingFormatsForEnumerationQuestions
payload.description: When a question asks what kinds or forms of writing or creative work someone produces (an enumeration, not only the current project), run searches with generic format terms and include completed or published works.
content: When a question asks what kinds or forms of writing a person produces (e.g., what do they write, what formats they work in), treat it as an enumeration of all their writing types, not just their current project.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search using generic format terms such as 'writings', 'published', 'blog', 'essay', 'journal', 'story', 'book', 'script', or 'screenplay' rather than only 'currently working on' or project-specific phrases.
Include event memories describing completed works or works that received outside responses (performed, published, read by others), not only memories about current projects.

candidates.solves: Enumeration questions about a person's writing formats were answered from current-project searches, missing completed formats stored as events (e.g., a performed screenplay, a blog post read by others). The rule adds a second search using generic format terms and accepts completed-work events as evidence. Applies to future 'what kinds of writings/creative works does X produce' questions; not to questions explicitly about the current ongoing project.

payload.name: Expand-synonyms-when-counting-work-outcomes
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many times a person's work or creative output was rejected or received a repeated outcome, and memories may describe the work with different nouns.
content: When counting repeated outcomes for a person's work (e.g., how many times rejected, accepted, submitted), do not limit queries to the exact noun in the question; include synonyms and broader descriptions such as 'creative work', 'submission', 'project', or 'screenplay' when the question says 'scripts'.

Include derived noun forms of the outcome verb (e.g., 'rejection', 'decline') and phrases like 'another rejection', 'setback', or 'turned down' in keyword searches, not only verb inflections like 'rejected'.
After finding an initial matching event, run at least one additional search with the broader object terms before answering, and enumerate every distinct event memory that matches the asked outcome.

candidates.solves: The agent found only one rejection because its queries used only the literal noun 'scripts', missing a memory about 'another rejection ... for her creative work'. Counting repeated events requires synonym and broader-object searches anchored on the person, not just verb inflections from the question. Applies to future count questions about repeated outcomes for a person's work when memories phrase the object differently.

payload.name: IncludeCommunityWritingInCreativeWorkSearch
payload.description: When a question asks what kind of writing or creative work someone does, search for community participation (forum posts, comments, discussions, reviews) in addition to formal writing projects before answering.
content: When a question asks what kind of writing or creative content someone produces, do not limit queries to 'writing', 'articles', 'stories', or 'novel'; include community-writing terms such as 'forum', 'comments', 'discussion', 'posts', and 'reviews' in query expansions and keywords.

Treat memories about joining an online community, discussion group, or forum and sharing thoughts on favorite topics as potential evidence of that person's writing, even when the memory does not contain the word 'write' or 'writing'.

If the initial search returns only formal writing projects (e.g., articles, books), run at least one additional search targeting community participation before answering, so comments and reviews are not omitted.

candidates.solves: When a question asks broadly what kind of writing or creative work someone does, retrieval can miss community-writing activities (forum posts, comments, discussions, reviews) because queries target formal terms like 'articles' or 'novel'. This skill expands search vocabulary to text-producing community activities and accepts participation memories as writing evidence, ensuring complete answers; it is not needed when the question targets one specific formal work or genre.

payload.name: Include ongoing-profile memories for time-bound improvement questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did during a specific time period to improve or care for something (health, pets, skills), retrieve profile/relationship memories too, not just event memories in that date range.
content: If a question asks what <person> did in <month/period> to <improve/care for/manage> <subject>, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; the supporting memory may be a 'profile' memory describing an ongoing membership, class, routine, or group participation that lacks an event date inside that period.

Run at least one search with memory_kinds including 'profile' (plus 'event' and, for planned actions, 'plan'), and do not require world_start to fall within the target month; ongoing profile facts remain valid evidence for actions taken during the period.

Before answering, if the event-only search returns activities but a profile memory explicitly states an action that matches the question (e.g., participates/joined/attends), prefer or include that memory as direct evidence rather than concluding with a list of related events.

candidates.solves: When a time-bounded 'what did X do to improve/care for Y' query retrieves only event memories near the dates, it can miss durable facts stored as profile memories (e.g., group membership, class enrollment). The failure is over-restriction to event kind and exact date window. Rule: for such queries, also retrieve profile memories and accept ongoing facts as evidence. Applies to future questions about actions, routines, or participation in a given period.

payload.name: Locate milestone date before post-milestone retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did after a milestone (e.g., after returning from a trip) but the milestone date is not stated, find the explicit event memory of that milestone first and use its date as the temporal anchor.
content: If a question asks what someone did after a milestone without giving its date, do not infer the date from a plan or preference memory that merely mentions the trip or event; first search for an explicit event memory recording the return or milestone completion and use its world_start as the anchor.

When searching for the follow-up event, include relationship/group synonyms and reunion vocabulary (team/teammates, reunited, met, gathered) instead of repeating only the question wording; the supporting memory may express the event with different terms.
Before answering, verify the candidate follow-up memory is dated on or after the milestone date; if all candidates predate it, re-search with the confirmed milestone date before answering.

candidates.solves: The agent failed by anchoring on a plan memory mentioning the trip, using it as the milestone date, and picking a follow-up event predating it. Questions asking for an event after an undated milestone need the milestone date established from an explicit event memory before temporal filtering, plus synonym-based search for the follow-up event. Applies to post-trip/post-event retrieval when the milestone date is not stated; not needed when the date is given.

payload.name: Broad-period temporal retrieval
payload.description: When a question names a calendar period (e.g., mid-August 2023, early 2023, last month) and asks what someone did, joined, or attended, use a time-range or unfiltered search instead of a single point target_time.
content: When a question specifies a period such as 'mid-August', 'early 2023', or 'last month', do not set time_mode to a single point target_time; use a time range covering the full named span, or omit the time filter and filter results manually by world_start.

If the first search used a restrictive point time and returned no relevant evidence, run an additional search without that point time or with a broader window before concluding 'no information available'.
Treat memories whose world_start falls within the named period as relevant even if the memory describes the event with relative phrasing like 'a few days ago' rather than an explicit date.

candidates.solves: This solves cases where a temporal question names a period (like mid-August or early 2023) but the agent converts it to a single point date, filtering out relevant memories whose start date falls later in that period and then wrongly answering that no information exists. The fix is to search with a broad time range or no point-in-time filter, then judge relevance by whether the memory's world_start falls inside the named period. Applies to any future retrieval question about events, classes, trips, or plans anchored to a vague calendar period.

payload.name: Search interest and goal memories for future project questions
payload.description: When a question asks about someone's projects, plans, or initiatives for an upcoming period, use interest/goal wording in retrieval and inspect event memories with predicate 'project' even if they lack explicit future dates.
content: When a question asks about a person's projects, plans, or initiatives for an upcoming period, run an additional hybrid search using intention/interest verbs (e.g., 'is interested in', 'aims to', 'wants to', 'hopes to', 'focused on') with the person's name, without requiring the question's time phrase.

Treat event memories with predicate 'project' that describe current interests or goals as direct evidence for future-project questions, even if the memory text lacks an explicit future date; do not answer 'no information' until such interest/goal events have been checked.

candidates.solves: Future-project questions often miss memories that state intentions as interests or goals (e.g., 'interested in', 'aims to') rather than explicit dated plans. The diagnosed cause was retrieval anchored to 'next year', which the target event memories lacked. This rule abstracts that by adding non-temporal intention phrasing and accepting predicate-'project' events without future dates as evidence, applying to any person/project planning query.

payload.name: Expand event-type terms for organizing questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks what event or activity someone is organizing, hosting, or planning in a time period and initial retrieval returns only unrelated memories; apply before answering to broaden query terms and resolve relative dates.
content: When a question asks what someone is organizing, hosting, or planning in a period, do not limit query expansions to the generic word 'event'; add synonyms for likely activity or event types (e.g., party, gathering, trip, competition, celebration) based on the person's known interests and the question context.

Resolve relative time expressions in the question or in candidate memories (e.g., 'two weekends later', 'next month') using the session timestamp, and set target_time or filters to the approximated calendar dates rather than only the month name.

If repeated searches with the same generic query return no direct evidence, run at least one additional search using the activity/object terms and the resolved date before answering 'No information available'.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what event or activity someone is organizing in a period, the agent may repeat a generic query with only 'event' and the month, missing memories that name the activity and use relative dates. This leads to premature 'no information' answers. The rule broadens query expansions to event-type synonyms and resolves relative time expressions to concrete dates before concluding absence of evidence. It applies to future organizing questions where the evidence is phrased around the activity name rather than the word 'event'.

payload.name: Date-unconstrained follow-up for dated acceptance queries
payload.description: When a question asks what professional experience or opportunity a person was accepted for on a specific date, and date-filtered retrieval returns no matching memory, apply this before answering no information.
content: When a question asks what a person was accepted for or got on a specific date, do not make all searches use that exact date: the supporting event may be stored with a different date (e.g., the internship or program start date) while the acceptance date is absent from the text.

Run at least one additional search combining the person with opportunity-type and acceptance terms (accepted, admitted, offered, internship) without the date filter, and check whether it returns a matching memory before answering 'no information'.

candidates.solves: Questions asking what someone was accepted for or got on a specific date can fail because the supporting memory stores a different date (e.g., internship start date). Future inputs with this dated-acceptance pattern should trigger a date-unconstrained search on the person plus opportunity/acceptance terms before concluding no information. Not applicable when the queried date is itself the event's stored date and no related memory exists.

payload.name: Verify event falls in requested time period
payload.description: When a question asks what event happened during a specified time period (e.g., 'during summer 2023', 'towards the end of August'), verify candidate memory dates fall within that period before answering; reject out-of-window events.
content: When a question asks for an event that happened during a specified time period (e.g., 'in summer 2023', 'towards the end of August'), check each candidate memory's world_start (and world_end if present) against that period before citing it as evidence.
If a candidate event's date falls outside the requested period, do not answer with it; run additional searches for events whose dates are inside the period.
Use the calendar definition of the time period (e.g., summer ends around September 22) and resolve relative dates from the session/memory timestamp when determining whether the event fits.

candidates.solves: The agent answered with an event dated October 15-16, 2023, when the question asked for an event 'towards the end of summer 2023', failing to verify the candidate's date against the explicit time window. The abstraction is that any question specifying a time period for an event requires verifying that the cited memory's date falls within that window; this applies to future questions about events in named seasons, months, or relative time ranges, independent of the specific topic or entities.

payload.name: Search preference memories for date-specific recommendations
payload.description: When a question asks what one person recommended, suggested, or praised to another on a specific date, use this to include preference/state memories and verify date-aligned evidence.
content: When a question asks what X recommended to Y on a specific date, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; also search or omit filters for 'preference' and 'state', because recommendations are often stored as preference memories whose world_start marks the mention date.

Run a supplementary search using the recommender's name plus recommendation intent terms (recommended, suggested, highly recommends, good) and the target date, and inspect preference memories even if they do not name the recipient.

Before answering, verify the evidence memory's time range covers the target date and the recommender is the subject; if the only match is an older partial event mentioning similar entities, continue searching rather than answering from that partial match.

candidates.solves: Date-specific recommendation questions fail when retrieval is restricted to event memories and the answering stops at an older partial event match; the correct evidence is often a preference memory with a world_start date matching the target date. This rule applies to any future 'what did X recommend to Y on date Z' query and directs searches across preference/state memories plus date verification before answering.

payload.name: Negative-event retrieval for period-quality questions
payload.description: When a question asks whether a date range or month was good/bad for someone's career, work, or creative pursuit, and initial retrieval finds no direct event, search for negative/setback vocabulary before concluding no evidence.
content: When a question asks whether a date range was good/bad for a named person's domain (e.g., career, work, creative output), search for both positive and negative events in that window, not only for the domain word or positive milestones.

If a structured date-range search returns no directly relevant memory, run additional keyword/hybrid searches pairing the person/domain with setback vocabulary (setback, crash, loss, poor performance, failure, struggled) and treat memories whose world_start falls inside the range as evidence.

Do not answer 'no' or 'no information' just because no positive milestone was found; infer domain relevance from the person's known activities (e.g., gaming tournaments, writing projects, work incidents) and cite those events when they support an evaluative answer.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed: a date-range quality question retrieved only positive career vocabulary and missed setback/incident memories that lack the word career. The reusable mechanism is treating negative or indirectly worded domain events as non-evidence. This applies to any future yes/no or evaluative question about whether a time window was good/bad for a named person's profession or pursuit when the first search returns no directly matched event; it is not limited to gaming or laptop examples.

payload.name: SearchIndividualActivitiesForJointActivityQueries
payload.description: When a question asks what two people do together (e.g., couple, friends, family), search each person's individual activity/hobby/interest memories, not only queries containing both names and 'together'.
content: For questions about activities two people do together (e.g., 'What do X and Y do together?'), do not rely only on queries containing both names plus 'together'; those queries miss memories that record a shared activity under one person's activity/event/preference memory without naming the other person.

Run additional searches for each person individually with activity-focused terms (e.g., '[Name] activities', '[Name] hobbies', '[Name] enjoys', '[Name] outdoor') and, if available, use structured search with predicate='activity' for each person.
If the first search returns only relationship/context memories and no concrete joint activities, retry with these individual activity searches before concluding no evidence exists.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what two people do together, anchoring retrieval on both names plus 'together' misses shared activities stored under one person's individual activity/hobby/event memories. This skill adds per-person activity searches so future relational activity questions surface such evidence; it does not apply to single-person current-activity questions, which are covered by existing memory-kind skills.

payload.name: Search recommendation terms for shared-item queries
payload.description: When a question asks which items (movies, books, games) two or more people have both seen, read, or played, use recommendation-related searches because consuming an item recommended by another implies both have experienced it.
content: After searching each person with consumption terms (watched/read/played), also search each person's name with 'recommended'/'suggested' plus the item category; treat a memory that one person consumed an item on the other's recommendation as shared experience evidence.
Do not finalize the overlap list until recommendation-term searches have been tried, since the shared item may be recorded only as a recommendation-consumption event.

candidates.solves: Shared-experience answers were incomplete because recommendation-consumption memories were not searched; one person consuming an item recommended by the other implies both experienced it. Future queries asking what a pair/group both saw/read/played should include recommendation-oriented searches before finalizing, but not apply to questions solely about recommendations without consumption.

payload.name: ExpandQueriesForTaughtOrSharedSkills
payload.description: When a question asks what skills or knowledge a person has helped others learn, taught, or shared, run additional searches using teaching/sharing language and include profile and preference memories.
content: If the question asks what skills or knowledge a person has helped others learn, taught, or shared, do not rely only on literal skill terms; run additional semantic and keyword searches using teaching and sharing vocabulary ('taught', 'teaches', 'shared', 'sharing', 'passion', 'helped', 'showed', 'tips') combined with that person's known activities and interests.
Include 'profile' and 'preference' memory kinds in these searches, because a willingness to help others learn is often stored as an interest or passion rather than an explicit skill.

Before answering, if any retrieved memory shows the person developing, making, or enjoying something while 'sharing' it or expressing 'passion' about it, treat that as potential evidence of helping others learn and continue searching until memories from all relevant domains have been considered.

candidates.solves: Use when a future question asks what skills or knowledge a person has helped others learn, taught, or shared; such claims are often stored with sharing/teaching/passion wording rather than literal 'skill' terms, and the diagnosed failure was an over-narrow query that missed an interest memory and under-answered. Complementary searches across profile and preference memories fix this. The rule does not apply to questions about the person's own skills or activities.

payload.name: Expand discussion queries with advice and offer verbs
payload.description: When a question asks what people discussed or what advice one person gave another, before answering, also search with advice/offer wording and include plan memories phrased as suggestions or offers.
content: If a question asks what X and Y discussed, talked about, or what advice/suggestions one gave the other, run supplementary searches using memory-style verbs such as 'advised', 'suggested', 'offered to help', 'recommended', and 'helped with', paired with both person names, because such exchanges are often stored as 'X offered/suggested ... to Y' plan or event memories.

When judging evidence sufficiency for these 'discussed/advised' questions, treat a memory recording one person offering help or suggesting a strategy to the other as direct evidence of the discussion, even if it does not contain the words 'discuss' or 'talk'.
Do not answer from a person's general preference or standalone advice unless a memory links that advice to a conversation, offer, or plan involving the other person.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what two people discussed or what advice one gave another, retrieval often searches only with 'discussed' or 'talked about', missing memories phrased as an offer, suggestion, or plan from one person to another. This skill supplements such queries with advice/offer verbs and searches the memory as subject-object between the two people, making it applicable to future interpersonal discussion, recommendation, and help-offered questions.

payload.name: Retrieve recommendations without recipient and with time range
payload.description: Use when a question asks what a person recommended/suggested/advised to another person (e.g., which city/book X recommended to Y). Retrieve without requiring the recipient in memory and use a time range for month/year phrases.
content: If a question asks for a recommendation/suggestion/advice given by one person to another, run a search using only the recommender's name and recommendation verbs (recommended, suggested, advised, mentioned) plus the object type, without requiring the recipient's name to appear in the memory.

When the question includes a time period like a month or year (e.g., 'in January 2024'), use a time range covering the whole period instead of a point at the start, so memories dated anywhere in that period are eligible.

If the first search yields no evidence, do not conclude 'No information available'; retry with the recommender and object keywords only, and inspect events from that person that lack the recipient's name.

candidates.solves: Questions about what one person recommended/suggested to another often fail because the stored memory omits the recipient's name and the search over-requires it. Also, a month/year phrase may be treated as a point time, missing events later in that period. This applies to future recommendation/suggestion questions with a recipient and a temporal range, not to interest-based recommendation generation.

payload.name: Search engagement events for favorite-item questions
payload.description: When a question asks for a person's favorite or preferred item and explicit favorite/preference memories are missing, search for recent or current engagement with that item category and treat event memories naming a specific item as evidence.
content: If a favorite/preference question (e.g., favorite video game, book, movie, food) yields no explicit favorite memory, run an additional search using the person's name and the item category without the word 'favorite' (e.g., '<name> video game', '<name> book'), including both 'event' and 'preference' memory kinds.

Inspect any event memories describing the person currently playing, reading, watching, eating, or recommending a specific item; a specifically named item in an ongoing or recent activity can support the answer even if the memory does not use the word 'favorite'.
When judging evidence sufficiency for such questions, a memory of current engagement with a concrete item may be sufficient if no other specific item is named.

candidates.solves: A favorite/preference question can fail when memory stores the item only as an event (e.g., currently playing, recommending) without the word 'favorite'. This skill applies to future questions asking for a person's favorite or preferred item in any category; it instructs retrieval to also search engagement events and treat a specifically named engaged item as evidence when no explicit preference exists.

payload.name: Expand favorite-entity queries with admiration and fandom synonyms
